problem: Object-goal navigation policies are trained on a fixed set of target classes and use class-correlated inputs (dense visual features, knowledge graphs), so they overfit to seen classes and fail on novel target classes.
motivation: Real households contain many more object classes than can be covered in training, so the robot must reach targets of unseen classes. The authors argue that overfitting to seen classes comes from class-correlated inputs, so they use abstract, class-unrelated inputs to generalize the policy.
key_idea: Feed the policy only a detection matrix (visibility, box center, area per class) plus the GloVe cosine similarity between each class and the target, processed with self-attention, so the policy generalizes to unseen target classes via semantic similarity.
insight: Class-unrelated abstract inputs reduce overfitting: the training curves show baselines peaking early and then degrading, while SSNet improves steadily. The ablation shows self-attention gives the main gain (SR 20.3 to 27.9 on 18/4 L>=1) and the semantic reward adds a small further gain (to 28.6 SR, 9.0 SPL). Generalization drops as the number of seen classes shrinks (14/8 split).
method: Task setup (ZSON): the training targets are seen classes S; at test time the targets are unseen classes U, given only by their GloVe embedding; success means the target is visible within 1.5 m.

Input representation: a per-class detection matrix [v, xc, yc, area] (from ground-truth detections) concatenated with the cosine similarity between each class's GloVe embedding and the target embedding; it contains almost no class-identity information.

Self-attention module: the matrix is split along the class axis and self-attention learns inter-class relations from the similarities and detections; the per-class outputs are concatenated into a 1-D vector.
LSTM + A3C: the LSTM stores action history and A3C outputs a policy over 6 discrete actions (MoveAhead 0.25 m, Rotate 45°, Look up/down 30°, Done).

Semantic (partial) reward: on Done, +5 if the target is visible and 0 otherwise; otherwise -0.01 per step, replaced by the max cosine similarity between the target and visible objects whenever that exceeds the previous max, which encourages the agent to approach semantically related objects.
Baselines built for the task: a Random agent, MJOLNIR retrained under the zero-shot split, and ZS-Baseline (ResNet visual feature + target embedding + LSTM/A3C).

setting.backbone: SSNet: self-attention + LSTM + A3C (trained from scratch with RL); GloVe embeddings
setting.training_data: 80 AI2-THOR training rooms, 900,000 episodes on offline AI2-THOR data, seen target classes only (18 or 14 of the 22 classes); no extra data
setting.observation: RGB in AI2-THOR, but the policy consumes only a ground-truth detection matrix plus cosine similarities of GloVe embeddings
setting.action_space: discrete: MoveAhead 0.25 m, RotateLeft/Right 45°, LookUp/Down 30°, Done
setting.privileged: ground-truth object detection results used as a perfect detector

numbers_note: Table I also reports seen-class targets: 18/4 L>=1 SR 59.0 SPL 19.7 and 14/8 L>=1 SR 59.3 SPL 24.5. Only AI2-THOR is evaluated, and it is not one of the canonical benchmarks.
results: SSNet beats Random, ZS-Baseline and retrained MJOLNIR on unseen classes for both splits: 28.6 vs 20.7 SR (L>=1) on 18/4 and 21.5 vs 12.3 on 14/8. It also beats them on seen classes. In the normal setting, SR is slightly below MJOLNIR (63.7 vs 65.3) but SPL is higher (22.8 vs 21.1).
limitations: Only simulated AI2-THOR with simple room layouts; no real-robot validation
Relies on ground-truth detections instead of a real object detector
Generalization degrades as the number of seen classes shrinks, and absolute unseen SR remains low (~21-29%)
